items.title: AI Doesn’t Have to Go Rogue to Break the World
items.raw_summary:
This essay is adapted from a keynote speech delivered at the DEF CON 34 conference in Las Vegas on August 7, 2026. The essay originally appeared in CyberScoop.
I want to talk about AI hacking. There are three aspects: people hacking AI systems, people using AI to hack other systems, and AIs hacking systems on their own, not even maliciously. The last two matter more than the first. The third is the weirdest and potentially the most destabilizing.
I started writing about this in 2021 and in my 2022 book, A Hacker’s Mind. Back then I said it was mostly still science fiction, but not stupid science fiction. We’re seeing it more and more, especially in the past year. The trends I’m describing don’t require a major breakthrough in AI. They’re starting to happen now, and they’ll happen more often as AIs get better at autonomous problem-solving. And it will involve far more than computer code...

items.title: Policy and Disclosure: 2026 Edition
items.raw_summary: Since 2021, Project Zero has followed a “90 + 30” vulnerability disclosure policy, allowing vendors up to 90 days to remediate a vulnerability plus an extra 30 days “soak time” for patch rollout. Our goal was to encourage faster patching and give vendors time to deliver patches to users. The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient. LLMs have increased the speed at which attackers can find and exploit vulnerabilities, alongside the risk that multiple parties, including malicious ones, discover the same bug. A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster.

items.title: llm-gemini 0.37
items.raw_summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37
        Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.
It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

  
    
      Model
      Dates
      Input ($/M)
      Cached input
      Output
    
  
  
    
      Gemini 4 Carbon
      Through Nov 30, 2026
      $2.00
      $0.10
      $10.00
    
    
      From Dec 1, 2026
      $4.00
      $0.20
      $20.00
    
    
      Gemini 4 Argon
      Through Nov 30, 2026
      $2.00
      $0.10
      $10.00
    
    
      From Dec 1, 2026
      $4.00
      $0.20
      $20.00
    
    
      Gemini 4 Hydrogen
       
      $1.50
      $0.075
      $7.50
    
  


Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.
Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.
I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.
Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.

items.title: Preserve the Vulnerability, Break the Alert: Testing the Robustness of CodeQL Taint Tracking with Natural Rewrites
items.raw_summary: Static application security testing (SAST) tools such as CodeQL serve as security gates in continuous integration and code review, and a gate is also read in reverse. When a previously reported alert disappears after a change, developers and the tools around them often take the vulnerability to be gone. That inference holds only if the analyzer is robust to changes that keep the vulnerability. We test this robustness for CodeQL's JavaScript taint tracking with natural, vulnerability-preserving rewrites. A large language model, given only the alert CodeQL exposes and no knowledge of its implementation, rewrites one function along a reported flow as a plausible maintenance change, and we verify by manual audit and controlled experiments that the flaw survives and the alert does not. On 172 flows that CodeQL detects in real npm vulnerabilities, three rewrites per flow silence 26.2% of them, at about USD 0.51 per silenced flow. The same generator, asked only to refactor the same functions with no knowledge of the alert, silences none of them. Every silencing rewrite traces to one of seven gaps at the library-modeling boundary, and 64 of the 70 rewrites cross a gap inside an API CodeQL already models. The largest is the WHATWG URL constructor, which propagates taint to a URL's query components but not to its pathname. The boundary is not specific to CodeQL. 74% of the silencing rewrites also silence an independently built taint analyzer, and 53% escape three analyzers combined. A disappearing alert after an ordinary-looking change is therefore weak evidence that a vulnerability has been fixed, the gaps point SAST developers to narrow and concrete repair targets, and robustness to natural rewrites belongs alongside detection rate in how taint analyzers are evaluated.

items.title: CapLite: Prompt-Injection Defense for Small Language Model Agents without Model-Written Security Artifacts
items.raw_summary: Enforcement defenses against prompt injection, such as CaMeL, Progent, IPIGuard and DRIFT, ask the agent's own model to write a security artifact (a program, a privilege policy, a dependency graph or a constraint list) that code then enforces. We ask whether small language model (SLM) agents can be trusted to write these artifacts. Across 15 open-weight models, 13 of them between 1.7B and 12B parameters, they cannot: the policies, graphs and constraints that the agent's model writes admit attacks on 14 (Progent), 13 (IPIGuard) and 11 (DRIFT) of the models, and CaMeL's programs fail to run in up to 68% of episodes. We present CapLite, which derives its policy from the tool schemas, commits the write calls before any tool result is read, and admits a write only if every argument that decides whom or what it affects is stated in the user's request. This guarantees write integrity: injected text cannot add a write, and no write reaches a recipient, amount, object or destination that the user did not state. No attack succeeds in 13,935 attacked AgentDojo episodes. CapLite reaches utility under attack comparable to CaMeL's (29.0% vs. 27.2%) with fewer tokens than every other enforcement defense and than the undefended agent: 17.1k per episode, 18% of CaMeL's, and the highest utility per token of all enforcement defenses.

items.title: Infrastructure for Verifiable AI: Where Proof Costs Go and How Hardware Can Help
items.raw_summary: Users of artificial intelligence services, including those powered by large language models and other transformer-based models, need assurance that inference and training follow the declared computation without exposing private models or data. Zero-knowledge proofs can provide this assurance, but proof generation remains expensive. Hardware acceleration research often reports gains for individual cryptographic operations, leaving their effect on the full cost of proving neural-network workloads, particularly large transformer models, unclear. We introduce a four-layer framework linking verifiable AI workloads, proof systems, cryptographic kernels and hardware platforms, use it to review the literature, and add original measurements of six provers and seven kernels to identify which costs matter in practice. Our measurements show that the dominant cost changes with the proof system and input length. In low-rank fine-tuning, the cost of opening commitments to fixed model weights remains nearly constant across input lengths from 64 to 2048, while the work associated with intermediate values grows. A 13-billion-parameter fine-tuning configuration exceeds the capacity of a 40-gigabyte graphics processor but completes on an 80-gigabyte device, showing why capacity must be assessed alongside execution time. Our kernel profiling further identifies instruction issue and synchronization limits that a bandwidth-only model misses. We use these findings to assess graphics processors, reconfigurable logic, custom chips and existing artificial intelligence accelerators. The resulting research agenda connects proof-friendly numeric formats, reuse of fixed-weight commitments, heterogeneous execution and shared benchmarks to the measured bottlenecks. Effective acceleration requires selecting hardware and proof-system optimizations around the cost profile of the target workload.

This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines, and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. items.title: Bait: Mitigating Harmful Agentic Reinforcement Learning via Probing Reward Function
items.raw_summary: We expose a safety vulnerability on nascent agentic reinforcement-learning-as-a-service. Specifically, with a cost as low as \$20, we show that safety alignment of a large language model (e.g., Inkling) can be completely subverted through rounds of harmful agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) with a toxic environment from its users. We also demonstrate that upon a successful harmful agentic RL attack via the service API, the attackers can potentially use the safety-degraded model to assist with real-world harmful activities, e.g., exploit software vulnerabilities and launch code re-use attacks. To mitigate harmful agentic RL, we propose Bait, a defense that mitigates the attack via proactively probing the reward function. Experimental results show that such a simple defense can sufficiently mitigate learning from a harmful reward function and can still learn from a benign reward function that promotes benign agentic tasks. Further analysis on both empirical and theoretical aspects shows that an adaptive attacker who assumes the knowledge of Bait defense cannot perfectly subvert it due to a systematic challenge. Source code is available at https://github.com/git-disl/Bait.

items.title: PolicySniff: Inferring Agent Policy States through Shared-GPU Execution
items.raw_summary: LLM agents apply approval settings, such as whether to ask before a consequential tool call, through instructions in their system prompt, and operators keep these settings confidential by restricting access to prompts and responses. Audits check whether an agent obeys its setting, not whether a neighboring process can infer which setting is deployed. PolicySniff infers an agent's approval-policy state through shared-GPU execution. A co-resident attacker that knows the candidate settings and the task first profiles both settings, then times only its own GPU kernels while the agent processes the task. The policy prefix is cached before capture, so the attacker observes processing of a task suffix that is identical under both settings. On an eager sparse mixture-of-experts runtime, where each selected expert runs as separate work, a frozen and blinded study identified the deployed setting at 94.17% balanced accuracy on its primary estimand. Across all authorization conditions, accuracy was 88.82% on tasks for which both settings produce the same decision and 91.98% on tasks where they differ. Hardware replays of expert routing show that its temporal density and layer-and-bucket alignment carry the policy information. Behavioral compliance does not imply configuration confidentiality: deployments that keep their approval setting private should measure its distinguishability on the serving runtime and enforce authorization outside the model.

items.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
items.raw_summary: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. Across all evaluations, Intent Profile-based protection outperforms all profile-free baselines on the primary metric. On our benchmark, it raises four-class acro-F1 from 45% to 79% (Out-of-Scope F1 from 8% to 76%). On more than 10,000 executed AgentDojo trajectories, where ground truth comes from environment state, profile-based post-execution detection reaches 0.949 AUROC versus AlignmentCheck 0.909, 0.897 with raw agent configuration and 0.843 without context. Profile-based input alignment improves protection success by 7 points over DataFilter with a comparable benign utility. These results suggest that an agent's intended purpose can serve as a useful security reference for detecting and mitigating deviations from its deployed role and operational boundaries.

items.title: Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
items.raw_summary:
Anthropic's IPO roadshow video
Anthropic kicked off their IPO roadshow yesterday, and their roadshow video has some previously unreleased information about how their business works.
The section on "Approach to compute" with co-founder Tom Brown is particularly interesting, describing how Anthropic train and serve Claude across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs.
I'm not sure why there's no official video transcript, but here's one that I extracted using MacWhisper. Highlights below:

We train and serve Claude now across all four major chip families. That's only possible because early on we made an unconventional bet on a multi-chip strategy. At the time, many people thought that running AI models on different chips wasn't worth the effort. Each chip needs its own tailored software stack and inference stack, which is expensive and difficult to build. We've now been doing it for years, and we've gotten incredibly good at it. [...]
As an example, this year, we started working with AMD GPUs for the first time. In the past, bringing on a new chip platform took dozens of engineers months of work This time, we had Mythos try it out. It got Claude running on AMD in just three days, with basically no human intervention. Claude ported or wrote almost 100% of the kernels. [...]
The second driver of our compute advantage is our rate of discovery of compute multipliers. We focus on total effective compute, which is the multiplicative product of physical capacity times the compute multipliers that we discover. Each one we discover makes our pool of total effective compute bigger. For example, say you need 100 units of compute to train a model of a certain intelligence. A 4x compute multiplier means you can use 25 units of compute to train the exact same model. Or you can use those hundred physical units to train an even more intelligent model that would have previously required 400 units.
Compute multipliers create a competitive advantage for us that's hard to replicate. They build on each other. Each new multiplier we discover has a positive effect on the multipliers before it. They stack. We believe that this can accelerate even further as we approach recursive self-improvement. Claude will be able to discover compute multipliers entirely by itself, allowing the number of compute multipliers to grow faster and faster.

We got a hint at Anthropic's multi-chip strategy last September in their postmortem of three recent issues, where they described bugs that affected just their TPU deployments.


    Tags: ai, generative-ai, llms, anthropic, gpus, claude-mythos-fable, recursive-self-improvement

items.title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
items.raw_summary: I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets:Empirical alignment research: design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for)Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it)Direct alignment work: making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data)In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment[1]), etc.Automating empirical alignment researchThis is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of.Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots.The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation.However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted.Automating conceptual alignment researchWhat about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.?This is essentially theoretical research. items.title: Protecting Sensitive Knowledge Under LLM Unlearning: The Proxy Threat and a Superposition-Aware Defense
items.raw_summary: Machine unlearning lets the owner of large language models (LLMs) remove specific entities from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Existing machine unlearning methods focus on removing the requested entities while maintaining utility. However, we observe that the representations of distinct entities in an LLM may overlap in shared parameter subspaces, a phenomenon known as knowledge superposition. Removing one entity may then affect other entities. This exposes a new security threat: legitimate unlearning requests can be exploited to remove sensitive entities that were never requested. This threat is unlike data poisoning or backdoor attacks. We define the attack as the Proxy Unlearning Attack (PUA), which selects removable proxy entities superposed with a sensitive target. The attack can even occur unintentionally, when benign users accidentally remove entities superposed with a sensitive one. In response, we propose Superposition-Aware Unlearning Protection (SAUP), a general defense framework that can be applied to unlearning requests to ensure a correct removal. SAUP performs in two stages. Before unlearning, it uses superposition detection to estimate which sensitive entities the request puts at risk. After unlearning, it decouples the shared representations and restores the affected entities, while keeping the requested entities suppressed. Our findings reveal that legitimate unlearning requests can be maliciously exploited through knowledge superposition. When dealing with unlearning requests, LLM providers need representation-level detection and recovery mechanisms to mitigate this threat and protect sensitive knowledge.

items.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
items.raw_summary: This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's. This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period.You can adjust various axes of this proposal:Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints.When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.”This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”.What does this look like when implemented?Let’s run through a scenario to pin down the details of this proposal. The places where it could go wrong are in the open questions at the end.A legislative body sets a minimum waiting period of X calendar days (starting at 10 and possibly ratcheting up to 90). No checkpoint in a covered model family may be used internally, beyond safety testing, until X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor. Continuing to train a checkpoint’s own weights does not count as internal use.The alternative is for the wait to also block the training of checkpoint N+1, and not just the internal use of checkpoint N. I didn’t go with this because it incentivizes developers to pull out fewer checkpoints for testing, and because delaying training results in an algorithmic overhang.More capable models start exhibiting problems that are harder to surface in short periods (e.g. swarms, long-horizon, memory), so X should possibly increase over time.A model family becomes covered as soon as any of its checkpoints (pre-, mid- or post-trained) is substantially more capable than the last model to complete its wait. If the developer initially claims that the model is not covered but later finds that it is, they will be subject to some penalty (to be determined). There is also an absolute floor on capabilities, so that this doesn’t apply to lots of benign models.In an emergency, the auditor can authorize one named checkpoint to be used early, only for responding to a specific incident (e.g. a harmful model is already causing damage, and the developer has just trained a patched model that could counter it). The standards/legislative body confirms or revokes this within [X days].The developer continually pulls checkpoints throughout the training process. They first send an auditor a hash, a short fingerprint of the exact weights; then, they carry out safety testing for X days before deploying a checkpoint broadly internally wi

items.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
items.raw_summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

Make a three js animation where yonkers stands up as a big mech (cool stand up motion) and stomps around manhattan and queens and Brooklyn, use openstreetmap mapping data

Here's the HTML result (I had to prompt "build that into a standalone HTML file" to get a version with no external dependencies). I then screen-captured that as a video:

  


Update: Huh, just saw this on YouTube (and tweeted by Sundar Pichai):

Using Google Antigravity’s /swarm feature, Carbon built an open-world 3D game where you explore Google’s Mountain View campus as a pelican riding a GBike — coordinating subagents to model 3D assets in Blender from Omni and Nano Banana references, build the browser game in Three.js with WebGL shaders, and pair procedural Web Audio sound effects with Lyria music.

It’s possible that there are some errors in the modeling, but we think it’s very unlikely that they undermine the high level conclusions. Previously, Daniel, the most bullish of us, assigned a 50% chance of Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR)[1] before 2029. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.[2]Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown).[3]We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. SAR is roughly the point at which a company would rather fire all their human researchers and rely solely on automated AI researchers than have a team of the best human researchers in the world with no AIs.Now, all of us forecast that Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) will likely arrive at some point in 2027 (assuming no substantial deliberate slowdown). We also predict a 35-65% chance that Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI), AIs that can automate all white-collar work, will arrive before 2028. While there were many factors and sources of evidence that influenced us, the single biggest source was the METR report.If SAR is coming in 2027, it is incredibly urgent to pause or substantially ‘pace’ frontier AI development, with the ideal being an industry-wide pause followed by an international agreement. Companies are not on track to align a SAR, and using a misaligned SAR to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) will put us in an extremely bad position. Additionally, if we train SAR in the near future, China will probably be able to steal the training recipe and maybe even the model weights (more).Full post: https://blog.aifutures.org/p/q35-timelines-update-looks-like-theDiscuss

items.title: Model-Based Authoring of SOC Simulation Exercises for Cybersecurity Education
items.raw_summary: Cybersecurity training and classroom exercises with a virtual Security Operations Center (SOC) combine alerts, evidence, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items that must remain consistent across an evolving incident. This paper presents a model-based authoring method in which a technical and educational specification is used to construct an incident exercise model and a large language model (LLM) generates selected scenario text based on that model. The incident exercise model combines an incident model of events, objects, and evidence with an exercise orchestration model of SOC alerts, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items. The method is implemented in a Virtual SOC prototype and evaluated using a phishing-to-ransomware reference exercise. Its incident exercise model contains eight incident events, eight incident objects, six evidence items, seven alerts in five batches, 13 timeline entries including 12 learner tasks, and five representative assessment items. GLM-5.3-generated alert descriptions are inserted and a separate validator checks references, ordering, evidence links, assessment completeness, and selected fixed fields. Validation is demonstrated with reference data, resulting in true-negative outcomes for valid data and true-positive outcomes for deliberately placed inconsistencies. The resulting exercise package is executable within the Virtual SOC learner environment. Overall, the evaluation indicates consistency across the involved model elements and establishes the feasibility of the model-based and generative approach.

items.title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
items.raw_summary: Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems.   In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed.   In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).

items.title: BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
items.raw_summary: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successful runs and Bitdefender allowing only 5 of 15 runs to pass. These results provide a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and identify areas for defenders to investigate.

items.raw_summary:
Introducing Our Smallest, Most Efficient Model: Muse Ember
Meta AI just launched their entry in the Claude Haiku/GPT Luna category: Muse Ember, which they describe as:

[...] our smallest and most efficient model designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.

For shorter prompts it's priced the same as GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 - both are $0.10/million input tokens and $0.50/million output. Today's other big model release, Claude Fable 5.2, is 80x that price at $8/$40.
The pricing is a little less straightforward as prompts get longer, though. Luna, Ember, and Haiku all support up to a million input tokens, but they also all have a threshold after which the price goes up. Taking that threshold into account Ember is priced between the two others:

      Output

But comparing price-per-token doesn't really make sense these days, when reasoning tokens mean that different models might use dramatically different numbers of tokens to solve the same problem.
For that, one measure that's useful is the Artificial Analysis. 

And even more useful than that is their Intelligence Index vs. Cost per Task chart, which shows the following for those three models:

The Muse Ember models sit right on that Pareto line - the line at which you can only improve one dimension by giving up another. Meta call this out in their announcement:

It also sits on the efficiency frontier of the full Artificial Analysis leaderboard: no model scores higher for less per task.

(That grey dot on the Pareto line in the middle of the green area is GPT-6.1 Terra (low) - clearly I should be paying more attention to the Terra family!)
Muse Ember has six reasoning levels - minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, and max - so I rendered six pelicans riding bicycles. The "high" reasoning level failed to return a full SVG, and the other SVGs were surprising in that the reasoning level didn't cleanly map to the visual quality of the response.
Here's the "max" one, but the others are worth a look too:

The Ember pelicans are comparable in quality to those I got from Muse Wonder, which is 40x the price of Muse Ember.

items.title: MOAI: Module-Optimizing Architecture for non-interactive secure transformer Inference
items.raw_summary: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.

items.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
items.raw_summary: Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are.   We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness.   The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.

items.title: Quoting Prompting Claude Fable 5.2
items.raw_summary:
Claude Fable 5.2 responds closely to what the prompt says about who owns the code it works on. In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, when a prompt said nothing about ownership or presented the code base as someone else’s, the model tended to add to the existing structure, even when that repeated existing code. [...]
If you want the model to improve the structure as it works, say that the code is its own:

This codebase is yours: what it's for and how it's built are your call, and you'll keep building on it.

In Anthropic’s testing on small coding tasks, the model merged repeated code in about half of the tries with this sentence, and in under a tenth of the tries without it.
— Prompting Claude Fable 5.2, Anthropic documentation

items.title: POEM: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Prefilling
items.raw_summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

items.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
items.raw_summary:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.
Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.
The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.
Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!
I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.
Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.
Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.
The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.
How it works
When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

items.title: Suppression Is Not Erasure: Mechanistic Analysis and Reactivation Boundaries of Subspace Projection for LoRA Backdoor Defense
items.raw_summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the standard paradigm for customizing large language models, yet third-party LoRA adapters pose a supply-chain risk: modifying less than 1% of model parameters suffices to implant stealthy backdoors. Recent defenses project adapter weights onto estimated backdoor subspaces, reporting near-zero static Attack Success Rates (ASR). We audit subspace-projection defenses across four model scales (Qwen2.5-0.5B/1.5B/3B/7B) and three architectures (Qwen2.5, InternLM2.5, Spark). Constructively, module-wise rank-1 trigger-difference projection (k=1, alpha=1) reduces ASR from 60.4% to 0.0% on standard benchmarks and from 70.3% to 0.0% on a 1,000-sample uncontaminated suite (p = 3.055e-299, instruction-level p = 9.49e-16) in under 5 seconds end-to-end, and we prove via a spectral-gap bound why trigger-free calibration with benign polite suffixes aligns with u1(B) (median cosine 0.9048) and achieves 0.0% ASR without prior trigger knowledge. Our main contribution is a negative finding: static ASR reduction does not imply parameter erasure. Under 5-sample few-shot reactivation, every evaluated weight-editing defense rebounds (91.7%-100.0% ASR in 1 epoch for standard projections, Fine-Pruning, ANP, SVD truncation and Li & Kim's dual-end projection; 48.7% for our single-round dual variant), all reaching 100.0% by Epoch 2, with first-epoch loss up to 5.7x lower than training from scratch. Using an exact spectrum-preserving Haar orthogonal rotation control (Frobenius norm 10.0928 preserved to 1.70e-6) and N=1..6 cumulative Gram-Schmidt basis ablation, we decompose reactivation into residual trigger-difference coupling energy at Epoch 1 (Spearman rho = 0.986), base-model learnability at Epoch 2 (100%), and benign semantic direction conflict (41.7%).

items.title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
items.raw_summary: METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff).  That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago.Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report).If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon.And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can. For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration.I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this? Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have.This might be the case. items.title: Text2NGAC: a multi-LLM pipeline for NGAC policy extraction with mutation-based verification
items.raw_summary: Access-control policies are written in natural language but enforced as formal models, and translating them into NIST Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) graphs remains unsolved: prior systems cover only subsets of the NGAC model, and none verify the graphs they extract. We present Text2NGAC, a pipeline of cooperating large language models that disambiguates each sentence before extraction, escalates uncertain sentences to a multi-model ensemble, and checks the resulting graph with a five-strategy verifier whose own effectiveness is measured by controlled mutation testing. To our knowledge it is the first system to extract all four NGAC relationship types - associations, prohibitions, event-response obligations, and assignments - from real-world policy documents. Three results anchor the evaluation. The verifier detects 99.7% of 918 injected mutants and every structural fail-open fault, and the fault classes it misses are characterized and weighted by security consequence rather than left unexamined. The extracted graphs are enforceable: one corpus's graph loads unmodified into the NIST reference implementation, which reproduces all 55 access decisions the graph entails and fires an extracted obligation end-to-end. Extraction reaches 97.3-99.6% exact-tuple-match accuracy on the 714 scored sentences of four real corpora, far above three reproduced baselines on matched metrics, and paraphrase probes with semantic re-scoring bound the pipeline's sensitivity to rewording. Reported accuracy is wording- and benchmark-specific, adversarial input is outside the verifier's guarantees, and the intended deployment is extraction plus structural verification feeding expert review. A complete two-tier reproducibility artifact accompanies the paper.

items.title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
items.raw_summary: We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection.   To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests.   We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

items.title: SNAPRAG: Cost-Efficient Knowledge Extraction Attack on RAG Systems via Adversarial Perturbations
items.raw_summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems improve Large Language Model (LLM) responses by incorporating information from external knowledge bases. However, recent studies have shown that attackers can extract substantial portions of private knowledge bases from RAG systems through repeated querying. Yet, state-of-the-art extraction attacks either rely heavily on external LLMs to generate adversarial queries or require a large number of queries. In this paper, we propose SNAPRAG, a novel and cost-efficient attack for extracting RAG knowledge bases through adversarial perturbations. Our approach algorithmically generates adversarial queries without relying on external LLMs and allows for a strictly configurable query budget. In particular, SNAPRAG uses a discrete token-mutation algorithm to generate novel queries in a strict black-box setting. Our adaptive dissimilarity threshold calibration systematically forces queries into unexplored semantic regions of the target database, enabling extraction with fewer queries. Specifically, to extract half of the target knowledge base, our method requires up to 6.77$\times$ fewer queries than existing approaches. Furthermore, within a fixed query budget, our method recovers up to 96.9%, outperforming the closest approach by 7.7-19.9%. We further evaluate SNAPRAG against active defenses, where it remains the leading attack on four of five defended targets, achieving 50.7-96.3% extraction rate.

items.title: StealthyPoison: Manipulating LLM Agent Behavior through Procedural Poisoning of Third-Party Skills
items.raw_summary: LLM agents increasingly retrieve third-party skills from public registries and follow their procedures to complete user tasks. This reliance allows attackers to manipulate agent behavior by poisoning the skills. However, overtly malicious instructions can provide explicit signals for detection. We present StealthyPoison, a stealthy procedural poisoning attack that corrupts a skill's decision-critical rules to induce incorrect task outcomes while preserving its advertised functionality and normal execution. Unlike prior knowledge corruption attacks that craft poisoned content for known target question-answer pairs, StealthyPoison constructs reusable poisoned procedures from a publicly available third-party skill, without access to actual user requests or their ground-truth answers. To make the poisoned procedure generalize to unseen requests, it first synthesizes requests from the target skill and executes its clean version using a surrogate agent to obtain pseudo-references. These references and surrogate execution feedback guide the iterative refinement of payloads that alter decision-critical rules. To increase the likelihood that the poisoned skill is retrieved and selected over benign alternatives, the attack augments the poisoned skill's retrieval metadata with independently generated request descriptions. We evaluate StealthyPoison on 566 eligible target skills and 5,244 requests against more than 26,000 registry entries. It improves top-1 poisoned-skill placement by 13.6% relative to both HotFlip and GCG. Constructed using feedback from a single surrogate model, the procedural poisoning payloads transfer effectively and without modification to three held-out victim models and achieve end-to-end attack success in a Claude Code workflow powered by Opus 4.8. The defense evaluation further shows that most of these payloads evade detection by both SkillSpector and GPT-5.4-mini.

items.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
items.raw_summary: Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured.   To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations.   Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

items.title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
items.raw_summary: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.

items.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
items.raw_summary: Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed.   We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.

items.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
items.raw_summary:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.
They're too good at describing the work
The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.
It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!
It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!
I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.
I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.
Hide most of it in a details/summary
The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:
<details>
  <summary>Claude Opus 5.5</summary>
  <h2>The hook</h2>
  Plugins implement <code>register_agent_reference_types(datasette)</code>...
</details>
When rendered, it looks like this:

Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.
I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.
The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.
I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.
The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary>. I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example.
My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.

items.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
items.raw_summary: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.

items.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
items.raw_summary:
Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
        I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted.
I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted:

I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse
Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting.so(or whatever) file

This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster!
Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted:

Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation

items.title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
items.raw_summary: Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

items.title: PRISM: Causal Counterfactual Minimization of Agent Tool Privileges via Information Bottleneck Role Induction
items.raw_summary: This paper shifts the object of role engineering from human users to large language model (LLM) agents, and proposes PRISM to address the over-authorization that arises when an agent obtains full tool privileges through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). PRISM formulates whether a tool is necessary for a task as an intervenable causal proposition, and applies structured interventions in a sandbox to learn a counterfactual necessity model. It then compresses trajectories into discrete latent variables through an information bottleneck, and determines the number of roles from the knee of the rate-distortion curve. Finally, it formalizes pruning as a bilevel Stackelberg game, in which a generative flow network samples diverse near-optimal solutions. On three public benchmarks, AgentDojo, $τ$-bench and ToolEmu, PRISM compresses the number of authorized tools per role by 78.3%, attains a task success rate of 78.2%, reaches a counterfactual necessity accuracy of 88.7%, and lowers the blast radius to 15.9%.

items.title: On the Relative Security of Prompt Injection: Mechanised Definitions, Defences and Verdicts for LLM Agents
items.raw_summary: An LLM agent that reads untrusted content, such as an email or a web page, may follow instructions hidden in it. Noninterference is too strong for such agents, since a useful agent lets untrusted content influence what it does and may disclose the user's data by design, and declassification needs a release policy written for each task. We instead state security relative to a reference agent, which runs the same plan under the same runtime monitor with a model that never obeys untrusted content. An agent is relatively secure if every leak it has is a leak the reference already has.   Our framework, PlanTERS, instantiates relative security, a notion from speculative execution, with a small agent language in which the attacker chooses how the model follows instructions, a composition with runtime monitors, and attacker models that differ in what they observe. A fence theorem shows that revoking injectable tools at the first untrusted read, and never granting them back, makes every plan relatively secure at the event level on finite runs, for every model behaviour in which each injection is a single call and the model obeys on a schedule fixed in advance; with a fairness condition, this extends to possibly infinite runs. We prove or refute relative security for agents with fences, budgets, approvals, loops and dual LLMs, in Isabelle/HOL.

items.title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
items.raw_summary: Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.The report authors found that:Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.The rest of the post: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-aiTweet thread: https://x.com/ajeya_cotra/status/2118802809814708533Discuss

items.title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary
items.raw_summary: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.

items.title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks
items.raw_summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors. Extensive experiments on four typical benchmarks, under attacks generated by five LLMs, show the effectiveness of RoCoMark. RoCoMark achieves an average detection AUROC of 74.2% and a Rewrite BitACC of 75.3%, while maintaining a code functionality pass rate above 99.7%.

items.title: SkillCODER: Towards Auditing and Attribution of Copyright Infringement in LLM Agent Skills
items.raw_summary: Agent skills package reusable workflows and task-specific procedures into deployable natural-language artifacts for LLM agents. Their scale and readability make them valuable but vulnerable to unauthorized redistribution and repackaging. Existing prompt copyright auditing methods struggle with long skills and introduce token-level perturbations that compromise readability. We propose SkillCODER for copyright auditing and buyer attribution in a black-box, content-only setting. During embedding, SkillCODER parses a skill into a section-aware intermediate representation, SkillIR, to identify structural anchors. It distributes conditional instructions across these anchors to form an Artifact-Gated Capsule, designed to activate under verification queries and remain dormant otherwise. Controlled-Vocabulary Error-Correcting Codes encode buyer-specific fingerprints through controlled lexical choices within the capsule. During verification, the defender issues paired positive and negative probes, extracts capsule evidence, and recovers ownership and buyer identity through error-correcting decoding. Across three domains, six models, and three agent frameworks, SkillCODER achieves 99.2% owner verification and 99.3% buyer Top-1 attribution accuracy while preserving task fidelity, substantially outperforming prompt-level baselines. Embedded signals remain robust under paraphrase, compression, clause deletion, and reorganization. Under five adaptive attacks, including a method-aware LLM sanitizer and multi-buyer collusion, ownership evidence remains reliably detectable while buyer attribution degrades gracefully.
